query: Which material can be used for improve the magnetocaloric properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Doping La(Fe,Si)13 with cobalt (Co) improves the magnetocaloric effect by enhancing the magnetostructural coupling, reducing hysteresis, and broadening the operational temperature range near room temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: Undoped La(Fe,Si)13 alloy with moderate magnetocaloric performance but limitations in hysteresis and a narrow operating temperature range.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled amounts of Co into La(Fe,Si)13 and iteratively optimize the alloy composition guided by co-designed experiments and simulations.
generation.conditions: Cyclic magnetic field changes near ambient temperatures (approx. 290–310 K) under practical operational conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced magnetostructural coupling due to Co incorporation, which modifies lattice parameters and electronic structure.
generation.mechanism: Co doping alters the balance between magnetic ordering and structural transitions, leading to a more reversible phase transition with improved entropy change and reduced thermal hysteresis.
generation.predicted_outcome: Increase in the magnetic entropy change (ΔS_m), broader operational temperature span, and reduced hysteresis compared to the undoped baseline.
generation.baseline: Undoped La(Fe,Si)13 alloy exhibiting prior moderate magnetocaloric effects and performance limitations.
generation.boundary: Valid within optimal Co doping levels; excessive doping may lead to phase separation or degradation of the desired magnetocaloric properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimum Co concentration and the quantitative magnitude of performance improvement are uncertain and need to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of La(Fe,Si)13 alloys with varying Co doping levels (e.g., 0%, 2%, 5%, and 10% by atomic percent). Conduct cyclic magnetic field tests near room temperature and compare the magnetocaloric parameters with the baseline undoped sample.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the Co-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in ΔS_m, a measurable reduction in thermal hysteresis, or a broader operational temperature range compared to the undoped La(Fe,Si)13 alloy.

decision.trend: Early magnetocaloric materials research has relied on expensive Gd‐based compounds and La(Fe,Si)13 intermetallics which, despite their good isothermal entropy change, are hampered by issues of tunability and magnetic hysteresis. In parallel, studies—such as the recent work on FeCoNiTi high‐entropy alloys (PMC11375712)—have demonstrated that tailoring composition can modify magnetic transition temperatures and magnetic anisotropy. This trend suggests that systematic compositional modifications (often observed in high‐entropy alloy and related magnetic systems) can be leveraged to achieve desirable magnetic transitions with improved cost‐effectiveness and reduced hysteresis.
decision.unsolved: The key challenge remains in designing a material that maintains a large and tunable magnetocaloric effect under moderate field changes, while simultaneously minimizing hysteresis and cost. How to control the magnetic phase transition temperature precisely and reduce the magnetic losses without resorting to scarce elements is still unresolved.
decision.lever: Tailoring the base intermetallic system (e.g., La(Fe,Si)13) by substituting a fraction of Fe or Si with abundant transition metals (or analogous 3d elements) to fine‐tune the magnetic transition temperature and lower hysteresis losses
decision.why: Building on the observed ability of compositional tuning in high-entropy systems to alter magnetic transitions and anisotropies (as exemplified in PMC11375712), this approach directly addresses the cost and hysteresis limitations noted in traditional magnetocaloric materials, making the material more suitable for moderate-field, near-room-temperature applications.
